title: Area XI review: Basic Instrument Maneuvers
intro: These questions mix the five Tasks of Area XI: straight-and-level flight, constant airspeed climbs and descents, turns to headings and unusual attitude recoveries, all taught under a view-limiting device. Many join two of them in one hood lesson, such as a climbing turn that rolls out and levels off together, a level-off that ends in an unusual attitude, a descending turn that becomes a spiral, or a compass turn on partial panel.

questions.q: You have just earned your CFI certificate, with no instrument rating on it. A commercial applicant asks you to give him the 10 hours of view-limiting device training, with partial panel work and unusual attitude recoveries, that 14 CFR 61.129(a)(3)(i) requires. What is your answer?
options: Yes, because 61.195(c) covers only training toward an instrument rating, and these hours belong to the commercial certificate instead
Yes, as long as an instrument-rated pilot rides along as the safety pilot on every hood flight, which satisfies 61.195(c) for these hours
Partly: you may give the partial panel hours, but 61.195(c) keeps the unusual attitude recoveries for an instructor with an instrument rating
No: 61.195(c) requires an instrument rating on your instructor certificate for the instrument training required for a commercial certificate
questions.why: 61.195(c) lets a flight instructor give instrument training for an instrument rating, a type rating not limited to VFR, or the instrument training required for the commercial and airline transport pilot certificates only when its requirements are met, starting with an instrument rating on the flight instructor certificate [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(c)]]. The commercial hours are that kind of training: 10 hours with a view-limiting device including attitude instrument flying, partial panel skills and recovery from unusual flight attitudes [[60:314|14 CFR 61.129(a)(3)(i)]]. The private pilot's 3 hours by reference to instruments are not on the 61.195(c) list [[60:300|14 CFR 61.109(a)(3)]], which is why a new CFI may give those but not these. A safety pilot answers 91.109(c), not 61.195(c), and the rule does not split the commercial hours into parts.

questions.q: To rehearse your Area XI talk-throughs under the hood, you plan to fly with a friend who holds a sport pilot certificate. He has sharp eyes and will sit in the right seat to watch for traffic. What does 14 CFR 91.109(c) say about this plan?
options: It fails: the safety pilot in the other control seat must hold at least a private pilot certificate with category and class ratings for the airplane
It works: the rule asks only that the safety pilot have adequate vision forward and to each side, and a sport pilot can provide that
It works if a competent observer also rides along to supplement his vision, because the observer makes up for the missing certificate
It works because you, the pilot flying under the hood, hold a commercial certificate, and the rule sets a certificate level for that pilot only
questions.why: Simulated instrument flight needs a safety pilot in the other control seat who holds at least a private pilot certificate with category and class ratings appropriate to the aircraft [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]]. Adequate vision forward and to each side is a second, separate condition, and a competent observer may supplement the safety pilot's vision, not stand in for his certificate [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]]. The certificate held by the pilot flying matters only for the single throwover wheel exception [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(3)]].

questions.q: Your learner levels off from an instrument descent at cruise power and settles 80 feet above the assigned altitude with the airspeed 8 knots below cruise. She reaches for the throttle. What do you coach?
options: Add power and hold the attitude: low airspeed at a constant power setting always points to a power problem, so the throttle is the right control here
Lower the nose a full bar width and reduce power, since both errors are on the same side of the targets and need pitch and power
Leave the throttle: with altitude high and airspeed low, a small pitch-down may fix both, so check the altimeter before changing power
Retrim nose-down and let go of the yoke, so the trim alone brings the airplane down and speeds it up without any control pressure
questions.why: If the airspeed is low and the altitude high, or the reverse, a change in pitch alone may return the airplane to both; only when both are high or both are low are pitch and power both needed [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]. The IFH says to check the altimeter before deciding a power change is necessary, because altitude can be traded for airspeed by lowering the nose [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]. An 80-foot error calls for a half bar width correction, not a full one [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]. Using trim alone to change attitude leads to erratic control [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

questions.q: After a climb level-off in a PFD trainer, your learner finds herself 300 feet below the assigned altitude. Using the IFH electronic display guidance, what rate of return should she set?
options: About 600 fpm, double the error, since the only cap is the optimum climb rate for that airspeed and configuration
About 500 fpm: double the error would be 600 fpm, but the glass section caps the rate of return at 500 fpm
About 300 fpm, a rate equal to the error, so that the return takes one full minute and stays smooth throughout
About 150 fpm, half the error, because any return faster than half the deviation counts as overcontrolling pitch
questions.why: The IFH glass section sets a rate of change of twice the altitude deviation, not to exceed 500 fpm [[23:155|IFH 6-22]]: 2 x 300 = 600 fpm, so 500 fpm. The analog section also doubles the error but caps it only at the optimum rate of climb or descent for the airspeed and configuration [[23:166|IFH 7-5]], which is the tempting 600 fpm answer. Both sections use double the error, so a rate equal to or half the error is not the rule.

questions.q: Your learner's straight-and-level flight and standard rate turns under the hood are now solid, and you want to add the AIH distraction of dropping a pencil for her to pick up. When do you drop it, and why?
options: With the wings level, because a head movement in a different plane during a turn can set off the Coriolis illusion
In the middle of a long standard rate turn, because the head-down pickup is hardest there and gives the most workload
During a level-off from a climb, because the inversion illusion there hides the head movement and keeps her calmer
Never under the hood, because the AIH limits hood distractions to radio calls and bans every head-down task outright
questions.why: Dropping a pencil for the learner to pick up is on the AIH list of distractions [[25:180|AIH 9-10]], given once the basic task is solid on its own [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. After a turn has lasted long enough, a head movement in a different plane can set the inner ear fluid moving and create the Coriolis illusion, so dropped items are retrieved with minimal head movement [[23:73|IFH 3-6]] [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. That is why the pickup belongs with the wings level. The inversion illusion comes from an abrupt change from climb to level flight and can make the pilot push nose-low [[23:73|IFH 3-6]], so it is a hazard, not a cover.

questions.q: Your learner has just leveled off from a descent to cruise by adding power first, as the IFH teaches. On the next climb she plans to level off to cruise the same way, power back first. What do you teach about the climb level-off?
options: It is the same: pull the throttle to cruise at the lead point, hold back pressure until about 50 feet below, then set the level attitude
It is the same sequence with a bigger lead of 100 to 150 feet at 500 fpm, because the airplane keeps climbing longer once power is reduced
It differs: lower the nose toward level at a 10 percent lead, keep climb power while the airplane accelerates, and reduce to cruise power as the speed nears cruise
Lower the nose and pull power to cruise together at the lead point, so the airspeed stays at climb speed until the airplane is level
questions.why: To level off from a climb at cruising airspeed, lead by 10 percent of the vertical speed, apply smooth forward pressure toward the level attitude, keep climb power while the airplane accelerates, and reduce to cruise power as the airspeed approaches cruise [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]. Lowering the nose and reducing power together is the level-off at climbing airspeed, which holds climb speed, not cruise [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]. Power first belongs to the descent: at the lead point add cruise power and hold forward pressure until about 50 feet above, and the 100 to 150-foot lead at 500 fpm is that descent lead [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

questions.q: Your learner climbs at 600 fpm in a standard rate climbing turn at 100 knots true airspeed, assigned 5,000 feet and heading 270°. She will reach both at about the same time. What leads do you teach?
options: Start both about 100 to 150 feet below 5,000 as one combined lead, because the turn adds to the height gained while leveling
Start the level-off about 120 feet below 5,000, double the usual lead in a turn, and roll out about 7 or 8° before 270°
Start the level-off about 60 feet below 5,000 and roll out about 15° before 270°, since the rollout lead equals the bank angle
Start the level-off about 60 feet below 5,000 and the rollout about 7 or 8° before 270°, using each lead on its own
questions.why: The climb level-off lead is 10 percent of the vertical speed: 600 x 0.10 = 60 feet [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]. Standard rate bank at 100 knots is about 100 / 10 + 5 = 15°, and the rollout lead is half the bank, 7.5° [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. No source gives one combined lead for a climbing turn that rolls out and levels at once, so each lead is used separately while the cross-check speeds up to cover bank as well as pitch [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. The 100 to 150-foot figure is the IFH lead for a descent level-off to cruise [[23:178|IFH 7-17]], and no source doubles the lead in a turn.

questions.q: Leveling from a climb under the hood, your learner snaps the nose down to level. A moment later she says she feels as if she is tumbling backward, pushes hard, and the airspeed starts rising with the altimeter unwinding. What happened, and what recovery order do you call?
options: The somatogravic illusion from acceleration; call the nose-high order: power up, forward pressure, then level the wings
The inversion illusion from the abrupt level-off; call the nose-low order: reduce power, level the wings, then raise the nose
The Coriolis illusion from a head movement; call for raising the nose first, then reducing power once the speed stops rising
The inversion illusion from the abrupt level-off; call for adding power first to stop the descent, then raise the nose and level
questions.why: An abrupt change from climb to straight-and-level flight can stimulate the otolith organs enough to create the inversion illusion, a feeling of tumbling backward, and the disoriented pilot may push abruptly into a nose-low attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. Rising airspeed with the altimeter unwinding is a nose-low attitude, and the IFH order is reduce power, correct the bank by the turn coordinator, then raise the nose with smooth back pressure [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. Adding power or raising the nose first reverses that order, and the nose-high order fits only a decaying airspeed [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. A smooth level-off at the right lead is the prevention.

questions.q: Twenty minutes into a long constant airspeed climb in a fixed-pitch trainer, the airspeed has crept 5 knots below climb speed although the climb picture on the attitude indicator has not changed. Your learner starts to lower the nose. What should she check first?
options: The tachometer: a normally aspirated engine loses power as it climbs, so the RPM falls and she must advance the throttle
The VSI, because a slow airspeed in a climb is always caused by too high a climb rate, which she should reduce first of all
The heading indicator, because gyro drift in a long climb puts the airplane in a slight turn that bleeds off airspeed
The miniature aircraft, because it should be reset to the new climb picture at intervals during every long climb
questions.why: Normally aspirated engines lose power as altitude is gained; with a fixed-pitch propeller the RPM falls, and the pilot advances the throttle to keep climb power [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. The tachometer or manifold pressure gauge is the primary power instrument in the stable climb [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. Pushing the nose down for a low airspeed that low power caused is a listed error; the fix is a faster cross-check of every relevant instrument before any input [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]. The miniature aircraft is set for level flight at cruise and not changed for other speeds [[23:138|IFH 6-5]], and heading indicator drift does not turn the airplane.

questions.q: In level flight before the descent, with the altimeter steady, your trainer's VSI reads 150 fpm up and cannot be adjusted. Your learner plans a 400 fpm constant airspeed descent. What VSI reading shows that rate?
options: About 400 fpm down, because a calibration error shows only in level flight and is gone once descending
About 550 fpm down, because the 150 fpm offset has to be added to whatever rate she wants
About 250 fpm down, because the needle's zero sits 150 fpm up and the descent is counted from there
No usable reading, because a VSI out of calibration is dropped from the scan for the whole descent
questions.why: A VSI out of calibration may show a climb or descent in level flight; if it cannot be adjusted, the error is taken into account when using it [[23:166|IFH 7-5]], and a reading other than zero can be referenced as the zero mark [[1:210|PHAK 8-8]]. Here zero sits at 150 fpm up, so a true 400 fpm descent reads 150 - 400 = -250, which is 250 fpm down. Reading 400 down ignores the offset. Reading 550 down adds the offset the wrong way, which would fit an offset that showed down. The instrument stays usable once the offset is known.

questions.q: Descending at 500 fpm toward a level-off at cruise, your learner adds cruise power 150 feet above the altitude and relaxes the forward pressure she was holding. The nose rises and she levels 60 feet high. What is the error, and what is the fix?
options: Too much lead: the IFH never starts a cruise level-off more than 50 feet above the altitude, so she began far too early
Wrong order: the IFH raises the nose first and adds cruise power only after the VSI reaches zero, so the nose cannot rise
Ballooning: the nose rises as the speed builds, so hold forward pressure to keep the descent rate until about 50 feet above, then level
Chasing the VSI: she should leave the VSI out during the level-off and fly the altimeter alone, since that needle lags
questions.why: Ballooning, letting the nose pitch up on a level-off from a descent because forward pressure was not held as power went in, is a listed IFH error [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. At 500 fpm the analog section leads a cruise level-off by 100 to 150 feet, adds cruise power at the lead point, and holds forward pressure because the nose tends to rise as the speed builds, until about 50 feet above [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. So her 150-foot lead was not the problem. The analog and glass sections both put power before pitch for this level-off [[23:211|IFH 7-50]].

questions.q: Studying IFH Figure 7-30, captioned 'Constant airspeed descent, airspeed high, reduce power', your learner sees tags making the VSI primary for pitch and the airspeed indicator primary for power. She plans to fly her constant airspeed descents that way. What do you tell her?
options: The tags show the constant rate method; in a constant airspeed descent any airspeed deviation calls for a pitch change
Fly it as tagged, because the figure is the official IFH layout for this descent and the text always defers to the figure
Use the tags only in turbulence, when the VSI is steadier than the airspeed indicator and so is better for pitch
Use the tags only on a glass panel, because the IFH electronic section makes the VSI tape primary for pitch here
questions.why: The figure's tags mark the VSI as primary pitch and the airspeed indicator as primary power, which is the constant rate method described in the text above it [[23:179|IFH 7-18]] [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. The text is clear that during a constant airspeed descent any deviation from the desired airspeed calls for a pitch adjustment [[23:178|IFH 7-17]], and the glass section makes the airspeed tape primary for pitch in this descent, not the VSI [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. In rough air the VSI is the less steady one: average its swings [[23:139|IFH 6-6]].

questions.q: Midway through a long standard rate descending turn, your learner's bank creeps steeper, the airspeed climbs and the altimeter unwinds faster. She pulls back and the descent gets worse. Afterward she says it felt like a straight, level descent. What do you teach her?
options: A somatogravic illusion from the entry power cut; the fix is full power at once whenever the descent rate starts rising again
A graveyard spiral: in a long turn the inner ear stops sensing it, and pulling only tightens it; shallow the bank first
A vacuum failure, since the attitude indicator always tumbles in long turns; she should cover it and fly the compass
An inversion illusion from the descent; the fix is to push to stop the tumbling feeling before rolling the wings level
questions.why: The fluid in the semicircular canals takes about 15 to 20 seconds to catch up with a turn [[23:71|IFH 3-4]]. In a prolonged, coordinated turn the pilot has the illusion of not turning; noticing the altitude loss, he pulls back, which tightens the spiral: the graveyard spiral [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. On the panel, a rapid fall of the altimeter and VSI with rising airspeed despite back pressure means a diving spiral, and the first action is to shallow the bank with coordinated aileron and rudder [[23:184|IFH 7-23]]. The inversion illusion comes from an abrupt climb-to-level change, not a descent [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

questions.q: Planning hood descents with a new private learner, you pick a practice area beside a busy nontowered airport so each descent can end in a pattern entry. Which facts from the midair study in the AIH should change that plan?
options: Most of them happened in IMC on instrument flight plans, so hood work in VMC near any airport adds very little risk
Most of them involved low-time solo students, so an instructor in the right seat removes most of that collision risk
Most of them happened above 3,000 feet in cruise, so a descent ending in a nontowered pattern lowers the risk
A flight instructor was aboard in 37 percent of them, and most were at or near nontowered airports below 1,000 feet
questions.why: In the study the AIH cites, flight instructors were aboard in 37 percent of the accidents, most aircraft were flying recreationally on no flight plan, the vast majority of accidents were at or near nontowered airports below 1,000 feet, and pilots of every experience level were involved [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Hood work also needs weather good enough to make up for the safety pilot's restricted view, with extra margin near busy airways or airports [[33:258|AIM 4-3-16]], and instructors tend to look inside too much during simulated instrument flight [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]].

questions.q: On one flight your private learner makes two 30° heading changes at 110 knots true airspeed: first a practice instrument turn using the IFH 'half the change' rule, then one during her simulated inadvertent IMC escape. What bank fits each?
options: About 16.5°, standard rate, for both turns, because the IFH and the AFH both use standard rate as their limit
About 15° for the practice turn, half the change and under standard rate, and no more than 10° for the escape
About 30° for the practice turn, equal to the change, and about 15° for the escape, half of that same change
About 10° for the practice turn, to stay shallow, and up to standard rate for the escape, so as to finish it sooner
questions.why: The IFH rule is about half the heading change, never more than standard rate [[23:213|IFH 7-52]]: 30 / 2 = 15°, under the standard rate bank of 110 / 10 + 5.5 = 16.5° [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. For a VFR pilot in IMC the AFH uses the smallest practical bank, never more than 10°, turning a few degrees, leveling and repeating if needed [[24:368|AFH 18-19]]. A 15° bank in the escape breaks that limit, and standard rate is the IFH cap, not the AFH one.

questions.q: Your learner is flying partial panel at 40° north latitude with the attitude and heading indicators covered. On east, she turns right to south on the magnetic compass with 16° of bank. Using the IFH method, at about what compass reading should she start the rollout?
options: About 212°, after the compass passes south, by the latitude minus half the bank
About 148°, before the compass reaches south, by the latitude minus half the bank
About 172°, half the bank before south, as for an ordinary heading-indicator rollout
About 215°, after the compass passes south, by 15° plus half of the latitude
questions.why: With 15° to 18° of bank, the lead or lag on northerly and southerly headings is about equal to the latitude. Turning to south, the IFH keeps the turn going until the compass passes south by the latitude minus the normal rollout lead; its 30° example from east starts the rollout at 203° [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. Here: 180 + 40 - 16 / 2 = 212°. The 215° answer is the PHAK rule of 15° plus half the latitude [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]], not the IFH method. After the rollout, read the heading only once straight, level and unaccelerated [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

questions.q: Your private learner climbs to an assigned 4,500 feet, levels off at 4,650 on a heading 15° off, and corrects. Then she flies a standard rate turn to 090° and rolls out on 078° at 4,560 feet, airspeed on target. How does she do against the Private ACS?
options: Both pass, since the Private ACS allows ±200 feet and ±20° after a climb level-off and after a turn alike
Both fail, since 150 feet and 15° are past the ±100 feet and ±10° that apply to every instrument maneuver flown
The climb level-off passes, but the 12° rollout error fails, since the Private ACS also holds turns to ±10°
The climb level-off fails on altitude, but the turn passes, because a turn is graded only on its altitude
questions.why: After the climb the Private standard is ±200 feet, ±20° and ±10 knots (ACS PA.VIII.B.S3): 4,650 - 4,500 = 150 feet and 15°, both inside. For turns to headings it is ±200 feet, a standard rate turn, rollout ±10° and ±10 knots (ACS PA.VIII.D.S1): 090 - 078 = 12°, outside, though 60 feet is fine. The ±100 feet and ±10° numbers are your CFI standard (ACS AI.XI.B.S3, AI.XI.D.S1), which you hold yourself to in demonstrations.

questions.q: Your learner rolls out of a long standard rate turn and keeps her cross-check going. The attitude indicator shows the wings level, but the heading indicator keeps slowly changing and the ball sits well off center. What does the IFH say is going on, and what should she do?
options: The attitude gyro has precessed, so she should ignore the ball and reset the attitude indicator before doing anything else
The heading indicator is precessing from the turn, so she should reset it to the magnetic compass right away, mid-turn
Nothing is wrong: after any turn the heading indicator rocks for about a minute, so she should ignore it until it settles
The airplane may be slipping or skidding in a turn: center the ball, check both indicators, stop the heading change and retrim
questions.why: A heading change while the attitude indicator shows level flight means the airplane is turning. With the ball centered the attitude gyro has precessed, but with the ball off center the airplane may be in a slipping or skidding turn. The IFH fix is to center the ball with rudder, check the attitude and heading indicators, stop the heading change if it continues, and retrim [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. The precessed gyro answer fits only a centered ball. A heading indicator drifts only about 15° per hour [[23:115|IFH 5-20]], so a heading that keeps moving is a real turn, not drift to reset mid-turn.

questions.q: Flying partial panel on a heading of 090°, your learner slows from cruise to climb speed and raises the nose for a climb. The compass card swings as if the airplane were turning toward south, and she starts a bank to correct it. What do you say?
options: Correct it: on east or west the compass always reads correctly, so any swing during the climb entry is a real turn to fix
Leave the bank: on east, slowing gives a false south turn indication; keep the wings level, read the compass once steady
Correct it by half the swing: on east the compass leads, so the real turn is about half of what the card shows
Leave it, since deceleration error shows up only on north and south, so the swing must be the climb attitude
questions.why: On an east or west heading, acceleration gives a north turn indication and deceleration a south turn indication [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. The compass is also affected by climbs, power changes and airspeed changes [[23:140|IFH 6-7]], and until the airplane is straight, level and unaccelerated its reading means little [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]. The tempting 'reads correctly on east' is the IFH turning-error rule for the start of a turn, not for speed changes [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. With the heading indicator covered, the turn coordinator shows whether the airplane is really turning.

questions.q: You set up a nose-high attitude a little too far. When your learner opens her eyes the stall horn is sounding and the airplane is buffeting. She calls 'nose high, power first' and starts to add full power. What do you coach?
options: Good: the IFH nose-high order always starts with power, and power alone ends the stall, so she levels afterward
Level the wings first with aileron, because the stall cannot be broken while any bank remains on the airplane
With stall cues already present, use the AFH stall recovery: reduce the AOA first, then roll level, then add power
Pull the power to idle first, then lower the nose, because the IFH reduces power first in every recovery
questions.why: The IFH nose-high recovery starts with power in proportion to the observed deceleration, then forward pressure, then bank [[23:188|IFH 7-27]], but once the stall warning or buffet is there the AFH stall recovery applies: reduce the AOA until the warning is gone, roll the wings level, then add power. Adding power reduces the altitude loss but does not end a stall, and the bank should not be fixed before the AOA is reduced [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Reducing power first is the IFH nose-low order [[23:189|IFH 7-28]], the wrong picture here.

questions.q: Your learner asks what minimum altitude the FAA sets for practicing unusual attitude recoveries and for the eyes-closed disorientation demonstrations you plan to fly first. What is accurate?
options: No source gives a number: the AFH asks for a clear area and enough altitude to recover, and the IFH rules out the demonstrations at low altitude
The CFI ACS sets 1,500 feet AGL for this Task, and the IFH applies the same floor to each of the disorientation demonstrations
The AFH sets 3,000 feet AGL for any upset training, while the disorientation demonstrations may be flown at any altitude at all
The AFH 1,500 feet AGL stall floor is written to cover unusual attitude recoveries too, so it is the FAA number for both
questions.why: The sources give no altitude for unusual attitude practice. For every maneuver with significant changes in altitude or direction, the AFH says to be sure the area is clear at and below and that sufficient altitude is available for a recovery; its 1,500 feet AGL recommendation is written for stall practice [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. The CFI ACS Task has no altitude element (ACS AI.XI.E). The IFH says not to attempt the disorientation demonstrations at low altitudes or without an instructor or appropriate safety pilot, with no number [[23:75|IFH 3-8]]. Borrowing the stall floor is an instructor's own choice, not an FAA figure for this Task.

questions.q: In a nose-low unusual attitude at 60° of bank, your learner pulls hard to stop the descent before rolling level, loading the airplane to 2 G. The trainer's book stall speed is 50 knots. About what speed does the wing now stall at, and what does the IFH order have her do instead?
options: About 100 knots, since stall speed doubles along with the load factor; she should keep pulling but add full power first
About 50 knots, since stall speed depends only on weight, not load; reduce power, raise the nose, then level the wings
About 71 knots, since stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor; raise the nose first, then reduce power and level
About 71 knots, since stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor; reduce power, level the wings, then raise the nose
questions.why: Stall speed increases in proportion to the square root of the load factor [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]: 50 x 1.414 = 70.7, about 71 knots, and a level, coordinated 60° bank alone already means 2 G [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. The IFH nose-low order is reduce power, correct the bank with coordinated aileron and rudder, then raise the nose with smooth back pressure; the instinct to pull first is the error [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. A startled pilot who pulls while rolling level in a steep nose-low spiral can create loads that damage or break the airframe [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

questions.q: A normal category trainer, limit load factor 3.8 G, is in a level, coordinated turn at 80° of bank because a learner rolled in too far while trying to hold altitude. What load factor is that, and how does it compare with the limit?
options: About 2 G, well inside the limit, because a coordinated bank never loads the wing past 2 G
About 5.76 G, roughly 2 G past the 3.8 G limit, so holding it could overstress the airframe
About 5.76 G, inside the limit, because the limit load factor for the normal category is 6 G
About 2.7 G, inside the limit, because load factor rises in step with bank angle: 80° is 4/3 of 60°
questions.why: In a level, coordinated turn the load factor is 2 G at 60° of bank and 5.76 G at 80° [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]], and it climbs very fast past 45° to 50°. The normal category limit load factor is 3.8 to -1.52 [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]: 5.76 - 3.8 = 1.96, about 2 G over. The 6 G figure belongs to the acrobatic category [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. Load factor does not follow bank angle in a straight line, so the 2.7 G guess (2 x 80 / 60) understates it. That is why the IFH nose-low order levels the wings before any back pressure [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].
